lead.t: A lung abscess is a localised area of necrosis of lung parenchyma with a cavity (usually 2 cm or more) containing pus or necrotic debris, caused by infection.

b: A localized area of suppurative necrosis within the pulmonary parenchyma, forming one or more cavities.
Aspiration of infective material from carious teeth, infected sinuses, or tonsils (during oral surgery, anesthesia, coma, or in cases of alcoholic intoxication).
Aspiration of gastric contents along with oropharyngeal organisms.

Complication of necrotizing bacterial pneumonias caused by organisms like S. aureus , S. pyogenes , K. pneumoniae , Pseudomonas spp., and rarely type 3 pneumococci. Mycotic infections and bronchiectasis can also lead to abscesses.
Bronchial obstruction , particularly by bronchogenic carcinoma, can lead to abscess formation within excavated necrotic tumor.

snip.t: A lung abscess is a localised area of necrosis of lung parenchyma with a cavity (usually 2 cm or more) containing pus or necrotic debris, caused by infection.
Large, dense opacity which may later cavitate and show a fluid level is the characteristic finding when a frank lung abscess is present.
Complications arise when exudate becomes loculated → Parapneumonic effusion / empyema, or when necrosis → Lung abscess, especially with *Staph aureus* or *Klebsiella*.

Parapneumonic effusion and empyema, lung abscess, sepsis and septic shock, respiratory failure and ARDS, pleurisy, pericarditis, lobar collapse, metastatic infection (meningitis, endocarditis, arthritis), bronchiectasis (long term).
Recurrent infection, massive haemoptysis, empyema, lung abscess, pneumothorax, respiratory failure and cor pulmonale, amyloidosis, metastatic infection (brain abscess), sinusitis.
Primary lung abscess: arises in previously normal lung, usually after aspiration.
Differential: acute bronchitis, tuberculosis (especially with HIV), pulmonary embolism, lung abscess, empyema, asthma or COPD exacerbation, and HIV-related pneumonia (Pneumocystis).

ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: A lung abscess is a necrotic cavity in lung tissue filled with pus, usually from aspirated oral flora or necrotizing pneumonia. Prompt diagnosis and targeted antibiotics plus drainage are essential to prevent severe complications.

sections.p: A lung abscess is a localized area of suppurative necrosis in the pulmonary parenchyma that forms a cavity ≥2 cm containing pus or necrotic debris.
b: Diagnosis requires imaging (CXR or CT) showing a cavity with an air‑fluid level.
Microbiological confirmation is optional but helps tailor therapy.

t.b: Does the image show a cavitary lesion with an air‑fluid level? Positive suggests abscess; a solid mass suggests tumor.
What is the size, wall thickness, and surrounding inflammation? Thick wall (>15 mm) and surrounding consolidation support abscess.
Which organisms are present? Growth of anaerobes or typical pathogens guides antibiotic choice; negative cultures do not rule out abscess.

sections.p: Severity is judged by size, systemic toxicity, and complications. No universal staging system exists, but clinicians use a three‑tier approach.
b: Mild: cavity <4 cm, stable vitals, no sepsis.
Moderate: cavity 4–6 cm, fever, leukocytosis, but no organ failure.
Severe: cavity >6 cm, septic shock, respiratory failure, or haemoptysis.

sections.p: Most lung abscesses arise from aspiration of oropharyngeal contents, especially in patients with altered consciousness or alcohol use.
b: Anaerobic bacteria from the oral cavity (e.g., Bacteroides, Fusobacterium).
Aspiration of gastric acid with mixed flora.
Necrotizing pneumonia (S. aureus, K. pneumoniae, Pseudomonas).
Bronchial obstruction by tumor or foreign body.
Fungal infection in immunocompromised hosts (e.g., Aspergillus).
Tuberculosis or HIV‑related opportunistic infections in low‑resource settings.

sections.p: Patients usually have a sub‑acute cough with foul‑smelling sputum, fever, night sweats, and weight loss.
b: Foul‑smelling, purulent sputum (anaerobes).
Fever and chills.
Chest pain that may be pleuritic.
Weight loss and fatigue.

sections.p: Imaging confirms the cavity; labs assess systemic response and guide antimicrobial therapy.
b: CBC for leukocytosis.
CRP/ESR to gauge inflammation.
Blood cultures if sepsis suspected.

t.b: Is there leukocytosis? Elevated white cells support infection; normal count does not exclude abscess.
Is CRP markedly raised? High levels indicate active inflammation; low levels may suggest a chronic cavity.
Are organisms isolated? Positive cultures identify bacteremia; negative cultures are common.

sections.p: Complications can be life‑threatening and require urgent intervention.
b: Massive haemoptysis.
Empyema or pleural effusion.
Septic shock.
Bronchopleural fistula.
Cor pulmonale from chronic hypoxia.

sections.p: Treat the infection, support the patient, and consider drainage if the cavity does not resolve.
b: Empiric IV antibiotics covering anaerobes and typical necrotizing pathogens (e.g., clindamycin or β‑lactam/β‑lactamase inhibitor).
Switch to oral therapy after clinical improvement (usually 4–6 weeks total).
Chest physiotherapy and incentive spirometry to improve clearance.
Percutaneous catheter drainage for large or non‑responding cavities.
Surgery (lobectomy) only for refractory cases or massive haemoptysis.

sections.p: Repeat imaging ensures resolution; address risk factors to avoid recurrence.
b: Chest X‑ray at 4–6 weeks to confirm cavity shrinkage.
Dental evaluation and oral hygiene for aspiration‑related cases.
Alcohol cessation programs.
Vaccination against influenza and pneumococcus.

sections.p: Several cavitary lung diseases mimic an abscess on imaging.
b: Pulmonary tuberculosis (especially cavitary TB).
Necrotizing pneumonia without true cavity formation.
Bronchogenic carcinoma with central necrosis.
Empyema (fluid collection in pleural space).

sections.p: Certain findings may give a false sense of security.
b: Normal sputum culture does not rule out anaerobic infection (fastidious organisms).
A small air‑fluid level on X‑ray can be missed, leading to delayed diagnosis.
Leukocytosis may be absent in immunocompromised patients.

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden worsening shortness of breath or chest pain

faq.q: Why is sputum foul‑smelling in lung abscess?
faq.a: Anaerobic bacteria produce volatile sulfur compounds that give a characteristic odor.

faq.q: Can a lung abscess resolve without antibiotics?
faq.a: Rarely; most require prolonged antimicrobial therapy, though small abscesses may respond to drainage alone.
When the cavity persists despite antibiotics and drainage, or when massive haemoptysis or bronchopleural fistula occurs.
